title: The TOADALNAEC and the Three Lies
subtitle: A ship that two sides agree is the same ship, a lesson plan whose third lie does the work, and a toad who got as far as the name
filed: 2 Aethel, 1040 BF — the morning after the session, from the screening desk
summary: A takeover that never says it is one, three lies that are really one rule, a pair of hands that were never shown, and the only compelled statement in the room cut off at a name.
thesis: The Toads did not take the ship by force or by argument. They took it by describing it, and the three lies of Archie Miser are a method for describing a man so that nothing he says can answer the description. The one person in the hall who said something unscripted was stopped in the middle of the sentence.

sections.heading: Both Sides Agreed on the Ship and Argued About the Name
sections.sourceAnchor: it may be the same layout
sections.body:
The first dispute on the gangway is a good example of how a takeover actually works. Nobody disputes the facts. The gate toad does not say the ship is a different ship. The party does not say the Toads are not aboard. Both parties concede the hull, the layout and the gangway. What is contested is the *possessive.*

That matters because a name is the cheapest thing in a takeover to change and the hardest thing to argue back. The Legion renamed the ship once, and the Toads have renamed it again. Each rename is a claim that the previous owner never had a right to the first one. If I am right, the TOADALNAEC is less a vessel than a notice, and the notice is addressed to the party standing on the gangway.

There is a second reading, and it is that the gate toad is simply right. The ship was seized by the Legion during the Iron Sky Breach. If the Toads have taken it back, then the old Vigilance was the Liberated Toads' to begin with, the party's claim is one that Disaster Inc. made on the Toads' behalf, and the gate toad is the only person at the gate whose employer actually paid for the paint.

I put the odds on the second reading. Hudston is called out because the gate toad cannot answer a claim to his employer's property. He calls for another toad, and not for an order. A man who expects trouble sends for muscle. This one sent for Hudston, who turned out to want a handshake.

sections.heading: Rivers Moved the Party Before He Told Them Anything
sections.sourceAnchor: I took over Speaker L's job while you were handling the whole manor situation
sections.body:
Look at the order in which Rivers does things. He does not argue. He announces that they are *new recruits* before any of them has agreed to anything, tells Dan to stop reporting to the Pond Patrol, and explains that Speaker L's job is his. Every one of those is a statement of fact in the present tense, and none of them is a request.

When a person is told what he is, the next thing he is told is what he does. Dan is not told to join the Toads. He is told he *already reports to Rivers.* The argument has been won in the grammar before it has been had.

The phrase about the manor deserves a second look. *While you guys handled the whole manor situation.* Rivers is saying that the party was occupied and that the post fell vacant in their absence, which is a way of making the vacancy their fault. There is no date on the change, and no vote, and no statement that Speaker L resigned. The archive holds one fact: Speaker L is now said to be in a cell.

If you remove the tone, Rivers has described a handover with no handover in it. I note that nobody in the hall asked for one.

sections.heading: The Third Lie Is the Only One That Does Any Work
sections.sourceAnchor: Anything Archie says is a lie
sections.body:
The three lies of Archie Miser are not three claims. The first two are claims. The third is a rule for what to do with every claim that follows.

The first lie is that he saved the Toads, and the correction is that he returned them to their place. That is a disagreement about how to read a rescue, and it can be argued. The second is that he is sane, and the correction is that he burned a village of orphans. That is an accusation, and it can be tested. Archie's answer is that the village never happened and that, on remembering it, it had been someone else. That reply is not a denial. It is the one sentence in the hall that sounds like a person checking his own memory and not finding himself in it.

The third lie ends the argument. It is not a charge at all. It tells every listener that whatever Archie says is false, and so his defence, his question and his offer to explain are false before they are spoken. I would call that the working part of the programme, and I would call the first two decoration.

It also fails in a way I find instructive. Markop's single question, why he is not fireballing the hall, is a claim that can only be answered by reference to something Archie does, not something he says. Rivers' reply is that Archie is afraid of him. The man in the barrel replies that this is the first time they have met. That is a statement a reader can check, and I have no evidence against it.

sections.heading: A Man Who Has Killed With His Hands Does Not Need to Hide Them
sections.body:
Rivers claims he fought, and that he killed *with his bare hands.* It is the only claim in the afternoon that can be checked in the room. Markop checks it.

There are three ways the hands could have answered. They could have been bruised, which supports the story. They could have been clean, which supports a hired killer. They could have been refused, which supports nothing. Rivers manages a fourth, which is to show the *floor.* He trips on purpose and holds up palms that are dirty from the fall.

The detail I keep returning to is the fake stumble. A man who has done the thing does not need an accident to show he has done it. A man who has not done it, but has a crowd and a deadline, invents a reason for his hands to be dirty and offers it for examination. It is a good invention. It would satisfy anyone who had not already said the words *bruised and bloodied.*

The answer about the chains is the cleverer one. *The metaphorical chains.* Nobody asked whether Rivers had metaphorically freed them. Markop asked whether anyone remembered being unchained, and the answer is that the unchaining is a figure of speech. I note that a toad says *makes sense,* and the hall does not object. I do not say they were persuaded. I say they were not asked to be.

sections.heading: The Only True Sentence Was Cut Off at the Name
sections.sourceAnchor: I also stole something from Archi
sections.body:
The truth spell did not fail. It did not reach Rivers, who was out of range and who answered a request to say it had failed by suggesting that Markop was a bad magician. It reached the toad next to him, who answered the first question put to him, and I think the answer deserves more weight than it has been given.

*I like lifting up people, and I also stole something from Archi—.* That is a confession in two halves. The first half is trivial and slightly charming. The second half is a theft, from a man the Toads are in the middle of calling a liar, committed by one of the people in the hall.

The sentence stops at the name. It is stopped not by the spell, which was compelling, but by a cup of tea poured down the speaker's throat. Rivers acted before the toad had finished his word, which means he knew what the end of the sentence was. A leader who is surprised by his own follower does not reach for a teapot. He lets the follower finish.

I record what I do not know. I do not know what was stolen or when. I do not know whether it belonged to Archie or whether Archie is merely the nearest victim. What I do know is that the dungeon now holds the only witness who has spoken under compulsion, and that the person who put him there is the Speaker he was asked to describe.

sections.heading: What I Would Do Next, and in What Order
sections.body:
The account ends with a man on fire and a hall emptying, and I will not pretend I know what happened next. I will say what I would do on the information I have.

First, find the toad in the dungeon. He said one true thing under a spell that could not be faked, and the end of that sentence is the only evidence in the file that bears on the Toads' own claims about Archie. Everything else in the afternoon is recitation.

Second, find Speaker L. Rivers says the Legion arrested him, the Toads recovered him, and the Toads jailed him. That is three events, and I would like each of them in the record from someone who was in a position to see it.

Third, treat the mask as unexplained and not as cursed. It was given free, it was refused, and within the hour Remi was turning Toads gold. Those facts sit side by side and I have no evidence that one caused the other. I would not move her to wear it, and I would not move her to throw it away.

Fourth, watch the crowd. They left. A hall that has been taught the third lie and has watched the man who taught it burn is a hall that is no longer sure it believes him. That is the single piece of movement in the account, and the only one that was not planned by Rivers.

verdict: Find the toad in the dungeon and ask him how the sentence ended. Find Speaker L and get his account of the arrest, the rescue and the cell. Treat the mask as unexplained. Watch the crowd: they walked out of the hall, and Rivers did not plan that.
